Description
The McCracken Lab at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi seeks a highly motivated and talented PhD student to join our collaborative and dynamic research team starting Spring 2027. This position offers the opportunity to conduct cutting-edge research on the Texas tortoise (Gopherus berlandieri), a species of significant ecological and conservation importance in South Texas. This research will involve a combination of fieldwork in rugged South Texas habitats, laboratory analysis, and ecological modeling, focusing on aspects of movement ecology, habitat and resource use, and/or translocation biology of the Texas tortoise.

About the Position
Primary Responsibilities:
Conduct field-based research on tortoise movement ecology using GPS telemetry and other innovative tracking methods.
Conduct habitat-use, resource-selection, and behavioral observations to characterize Texas tortoise ecology and inform conservation management.
Develop research questions and complementary study components within the scope of ongoing projects, while ensuring the fulfillment of funding agency objectives and reporting requirements.
Perform data analyses and prepare technical reports, manuscripts, and other deliverables for grant-funded projects.
Support investigations of disease prevalence and its effects on tortoise health, survival, and population dynamics.
Evaluate translocation outcomes and develop evidence-based strategies to improve conservation effectiveness.
Collaborate with state and federal agencies, conservation organizations, and private landowners to advance Texas tortoise management and recovery efforts.
Additional Opportunities:
Mentor undergraduate researchers in the lab and field.
Present findings at regional, national, and international conferences.

Qualifications
Required Qualifications:
Master’s degree in biology, wildlife ecology, or related field.
Experience with fieldwork in adverse conditions, particularly with herpetofauna or other wildlife.
Experience in data management and strong analytical skills.
Experience working with the programming language R
Strong communication skills (written and verbal in English) and a history of collaboration in professional team settings.
Demonstrated ability to work independently while contributing effectively within interdisciplinary research teams.
Strong self-motivation, professionalism, positive attitude, and interpersonal communication skills.
Valid driver’s license.
Preferred Qualifications:
Skills in GIS, telemetry, or statistical modeling are highly desirable.
Experience working with state or federal agencies, non-profit organizations, or private stakeholders.
Experience presenting research findings at scientific conferences.
Experience preparing manuscripts for publication or grant reports.
A passion for conservation and working in challenging field conditions.

What We Offer
Fully funded research expenses.
Funding opportunities for a competitive stipend and tuition coverage.
Access to state-of-the-art facilities and equipment.
Mentorship from an engaged and interdisciplinary team of researchers.
The opportunity to work in diverse ecosystems focusing on applied conservation science.

How to Apply
Interested candidates should submit the following:
A cover letter detailing research interests, career goals, and relevant experience (up to 400 words)
Curriculum Vitae (CV).
Contact information for three academic references.
Academic transcripts (unofficial copies are acceptable initially).
Please submit the above documents as a single PDF file Tortoise-PHD-LastName_Firstname].pdf and use ‘Texas tortoise PhD position 2027’ as subject line for the email to Dr. Shawn McCracken (shawn.mccracken@tamucc.edu). Applications will be reviewed on a rolling basis, with priority given to those received by September 14, 2026. The chosen applicant must submit all application documents by October 1, 2026.
Join the McCracken Lab
TAMUCC, located in Corpus Christi, TX, offers a unique coastal setting with access to diverse ecosystems and a vibrant research community. Join us in making a meaningful impact on the conservation of this iconic species and its habitats.
For more information, please contact Dr. McCracken.
Contact
Dr. Shawn McCracken
shawn.mccracken@tamucc.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
A PhD position is available in the Lichtenberg lab starting fall 2027. This position is part of an NSF-funded project that is developing a new framework and tools for understanding and valuing ecosystem services, with a focus on crop pollination. In collaboration with a computer scientist (Xiaohui Yuan at the University of North Texas) and another ecologist (Rufus Isaacs at Michigan State University), this student will provide ecological knowledge for development of computer vision (AI) models and conduct fieldwork to ground-truth those models. These models, and ecological theory, will contribute to development of the valuation framework by two environmental economists (Erik Lichtenberg at the University of Maryland, Kathy Baylis at the University of California, Santa Barbara). Additional project details are on the NSF awards page: https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/show-award/?AWD_ID=2617908.
 Research activities include fieldwork in Texas, literature synthesis, development of model training datasets, and contributing ecological knowledge to computer vision and economic model development. The student is also expected to conduct dissertation research related to this project or that leverages tools the Lichtenberg lab has built for working with species occurrence records. Preferred qualifications include fieldwork experience, ability to work in hot conditions, and patience. Funding includes semester and summer salary, a tuition scholarship, and health insurance. The Lichtenberg lab combines community and behavioral ecology to study plant-animal interactions, pollinator foraging and insect biodiversity. We are particularly interested in how land use change and land management practices affect these phenomena. The lab is committed to providing an inclusive and supportive environment to trainees from diverse backgrounds. More details at https://cos.unt.edu/biology/lichtenberg-lab/index.html.
 Application: Please contact Dr. Elinor Lichtenberg (elichten@unt.edu) before applying. Send your CV, information on relevant experiences, the degree and kinds of questions you are interested in, career goals, and unofficial transcripts.
 The University of North Texas is a R1 university located in Denton, near Dallas and Fort Worth. We are a Minority Serving Institution, a Hispanic Serving Institution and a Bee Campus. Department of Biological Sciences researchers study diverse topics, including conservation, sustainable production of plant-based materials, environmental education, remote sensing and neuroscience. The Lichtenberg Lab participates in the Advanced Environmental Research Institute, an interdisciplinary group that seeks to find solutions to pressing environmental issues. Denton is a vibrant college town known for its live music, and was ranked No. 1 Best Small Town in America. North Texas offers many opportunities for outdoor activities such as hiking, swimming, bird watching, wildflower viewing and horseback riding. Dallas and Fort Worth provide additional attractions, including museums, theater, restaurants and pro sports.
Contact
Elinor Lichtenberg
elichten@unt.edu (preferred contact method)

Description: We are seeking a highly motivated graduate assistant (GA) to develop ecosystem models and conduct analyses to address real-world challenges in fisheries and natural resource management. Our work is highly quantitative and applied, and seeks to understand how fish stocks and marine ecosystems respond to fishing and environmental change. In doing so, we aim to bridge the gap between ecosystem science, stock assessment, and management, while also advancing ecological theories and concepts. 
 This opportunity is open to prospective PhD students interested in learning to develop applied fisheries ecosystem models.  The graduate assistant will work on one or more projects that share the overarching goal of informing ecosystem-based fisheries management for the Gulf of Mexico and Southeast U.S.  Specifically, the student will use ecosystem models to evaluate fisheries productivity and develop effective management strategies in response to changes in climate, habitat, water quality, forage fisheries, harmful algal blooms, and invasive species.  
 The PhD student will be advised by Dr. David Chagaris and collaborate with a diverse team of scientists and faculty members from NOAA and UF.  The GA will join the UF/IFAS Nature Coast Biological Station (NCBS, https://ncbs.ifas.ufl.edu/) while pursuing their degree through the School of Forest, Fisheries, and Geomatics Sciences (SFFGS, https://ffgs.ifas.ufl.edu/) or the School of Natural Resources and Environment (SNRE, https://snre.ifas.ufl.edu/).  The interdepartmental arrangement provided through NCBS, SFFGS, and SNRE offers many opportunities for research collaboration, networking, and teaching. 
 Minimum Qualifications: MS degree in biology, ecology, marine science, fisheries, oceanography, wildlife, or related field. 
 Preferred Qualifications: 
·         Knowledge and experience with ecosystem and food web models, fish population dynamic models and stock assessment, species distribution models, and geospatial analysis of large fisheries and environmental datasets 
·         Strong written and oral communication skills, demonstrated by publications in peer-reviewed journals and presentations at professional conferences. 
·         Experience with the Ecopath with Ecosim ecosystem modeling software package. 
·         Proficient in R statistical computing software. 
·         Experience working in collaborative, multidisciplinary projects, and leading research projects. 

Salary: Annual salary is $30,000, plus tuition and benefits, including GatorGradCare health care plan, paid leave (5 days/per semester), and a voluntary retirement program. 
 Application Requirements:  Please submit a letter of interest, resume or CV, unofficial transcripts and contact information of two references to David Chagaris, dchagaris@ufl.edu. Applications will be accepted and reviewed as they are received, until the position is filled.

David Chagaris

Description
I am looking to fill a fully funded PhD assistantship in the College of Forestry, Wildlife, and Environment at Auburn University, beginning January 2027. Research in the Willoughby lab broadly examines how genetic and genomic variation shapes the persistence, evolution, and health of wild populations. Our work combines whole-genome sequencing, bioinformatics, experiments, and quantitative modeling to address questions in conservation genetics, evolutionary biology, and disease ecology. Additional information about our research and lab group is available on the Willoughby Lab website (https://willoughbylab.auburn.edu).
 The student will contribute to a newly funded project investigating brown-spot needle blight, an emerging threat to loblolly pine forests and timber production in the southeastern United States. This project continues a large interdisciplinary effort to characterize the fungi associated with the disease and understand its effects on pine growth and forest ecology. The student’s research will examine how genomic characteristics of pine-associated fungi, their responses to environmental stress, and fungal community composition contribute to variation in disease severity. The research will likely combine whole-genome sequencing, controlled experiments, RNA sequencing, and predictive modeling. The student will gain experience in fungal culturing, comparative genomics, bioinformatics, gene-expression analysis, and the integration of genomic, environmental, and ecological data. The precise emphasis of the dissertation can be shaped around the student’s interests within the broader goals of the funded project.
 The project is part of a large, interdisciplinary collaboration involving forest pathologists, geneticists, spatial scientists, extension specialists, graduate and undergraduate students, and scientists from Auburn University and the U.S. Forest Service. The ability and willingness to communicate across disciplines will therefore be important. The student should be interested in learning both laboratory and computational approaches and in connecting fundamental biological questions with an applied forest-health problem. Previous experience with molecular laboratory methods, fungal biology, genomics, bioinformatics, statistics, or programming is desirable, but applicants are not expected to arrive with experience in all—or even most—of these areas. Please do not self-select yourself out of applying. There are many ways to acquire the skills needed for a successful graduate experience, and the position is designed to provide training across laboratory, computational, and quantitative components of the research. More important qualifications include intellectual curiosity, persistence, a willingness to learn unfamiliar methods, clear communication, and the ability to work both independently and as part of a collaborative team.
 Auburn University is a very high research activity institution located in a mid-sized community in east-central Alabama. Auburn and neighboring Opelika offer a relatively low cost of living, restaurants, farmers markets, community events, and the Gogue Performing Arts Center. The nearby Kreher Preserve and Nature Center, Tuskegee National Forest, and other public lands provide year-round opportunities for outdoor recreation. Graduate students in the College of Forestry, Wildlife, and Environment receive a competitive stipend, tuition remission, and opportunities for professional development.
 I will interview prospective students before they submit a formal application to Auburn’s graduate program. Interested candidates should email Dr. Janna Willoughby at jwilloughby@auburn.edu with: 1) a brief description of their background and research interests;
2) an explanation of why this project interests them; and a PDF of their CV.
 Informal inquiries are welcome. Applications will be evaluated on a rolling basis and interviews are likely to occur no later than October 1, 2026.
Contact
Janna Willoughby
jwilloughby@auburn.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
The University of Alaska Fairbanks, College of Fisheries and Ocean Sciences (CFOS) is recruiting 8 PhD students to start in Spring, Summer or Fall 2027 through a new program called EMERGE Alaska.

EMERGE Alaska is a National Science Foundation (NSF) funded program for U.S. students who received an Honorable Mention on the NSF Graduate Research Fellowship Program (GRFP) during the last 3 years. The Fellowship covers stipend, tuition, fees, and health insurance for 3 years.

EMERGE Alaska focuses on marine and coastal ecosystem research, and is anchored on four components: academic training, research and innovation, professional development, and student success support. EMERGE Alaska is housed in CFOS, one of the largest and most geographically diverse academic and research organizations in Alaska.

UAF CFOS has three departments (Fisheries, Marine Biology, and Oceanography) whose 42 faculty and 138 graduate students work with local communities, Tribes, agencies, and the fishing industry, and do research from the Arctic to the Antarctic, including inland waters, coastal systems, and the deep ocean. CFOS operates NSF’s R/V Sikuliaq, an ice-capable research ship, as well as smaller research vessels, and has coastal research and laboratory facilities in Juneau, Seward, and Kachemak Bay.

The next deadline to apply is September 15, 2026. Eligible applicants must be U.S. Citizens, Nationals or green card holders who have already received the honorable mention. For more information and links to apply via NSF’s ETAP portal, visit our program website.

Description
The Watershed Management and Water Quality Lab in the Department of Animal and Range Sciences at New Mexico State University (NMSU) is seeking a motivated PhD student interested in watershed hydrology, water quality, climate impacts, and sustainable management of water-limited landscapes. This position is available for either the Spring or Fall 2027.

Research Background
Water scarcity is an evolving environmental challenge in the southwestern United States. Rising temperatures, prolonged droughts, changing precipitation regimes, extreme weather, wildfire, vegetation shifts, and growing demands from agriculture and communities are placing increasing pressure on already limited water resources. Addressing these challenges requires a new generation of watershed research that integrates field and Earth observations, computational modeling, data science, and management to understand not only how watersheds are changing, but also how they can be managed more effectively.

Our research group at NMSU investigates interactions among climate, vegetation, soils, land management, hydrology, and water quality, with a particular emphasis on semi-arid ecosystems. We integrate process-based modeling, remote sensing, hydroclimatic observations, geospatial analysis, and emerging data-driven approaches to develop science that supports agricultural productivity, ecosystem sustainability, and water-resource management.

Potential Research Directions
The selected student will have flexibility to help shape their dissertation around their interests and background. Current and emerging research directions within the group include:
• Watershed responses to climate variability, drought, and compound climate events;
• Hydrological and water-quality consequences of vegetation change, woody plant encroachment, wildfire, and land degradation;
• Development of Digital Twin and decision-support frameworks that integrate Earth observations, watershed models, stakeholder information, and data-driven methods;
• Development and evaluation of new agricultural best management practices, nature-based solutions, and precision rangeland management;

Desired Qualifications
Applicants from a broad range of backgrounds are encouraged to apply. Relevant disciplines may include hydrology, water resources, environmental science or engineering, agricultural engineering, range science, natural resources, geography, Earth and environmental sciences, civil engineering, or related fields. The successful candidate will be on Teaching Assistantship for the academic year and is expected to help teaching graduate/undergraduate courses in the Department of Animal and Range Sciences.

Strong candidates will have experience or interest in several of the following areas:

• Proficiency in hydrologic, watershed, ecohydrologic, or environmental modeling (e.g., SWAT, SWAT+);
• Watershed hydrology and/or water quality;
• Quantitative analysis of environmental or hydroclimatic data;
• GIS and geospatial analysis;
• Remote sensing and Earth observation datasets;
• Programming and data analysis using R, Python, Google Earth Engine, or similar tools;

Position Description: The Fowler Wetland and Waterbird Research Lab is seeking a PhD student to evaluate high-resolution seasonal movements of Black-Bellied Whistling Ducks in south Louisiana. This position will be advised by Dr. Drew Fowler at Louisiana State University through the Louisiana Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit and the School of Renewable Natural Resources. This project is funded by the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries (LDWF) and the selected student will work closely with state agency biologists and additional university researchers on the project. 

Black-Bellied Whistling Ducks (BBWD) have undergone rapid population growth and range expansion over the past two decades. In south Louisiana, commercial grain elevators receive extensive year-round use by BBWD and current abundances are a concern for food-safety and commercial shipping operations. This project will capture and mark individual BBWD with satellite telemetry devices at grain elevators as well as in rural landscapes to evaluate seasonal movements and habitat use, regional connectivity, and exposure and vulnerability to harvest.  Additional opportunities for research also include assessing response to hazing practices at grain elevators as well as evaluating dispersal and migratory behavior.

The student will work with Dr. Robert McCleery (University of Florida) and Dr. Mike Conner (Jones Center at Ichauway), with all field research conducted at the Jones Center at Ichauway in southwestern Georgia. 

The project 
Rodent populations can undergo dramatic changes in abundance over relatively short periods, yet we still have a limited understanding of how these fluctuations propagate through ecological communities. This project will use a large-scale manipulative field experiment with cotton rats to determine how major shifts in rodent abundance influence other components of the ecosystem. 

The student will experimentally manipulate cotton rat populations and quantify responses across multiple trophic levels, including: 
predators
Birds and other prey species
vegetation
insect communities
The project provides an opportunity to conduct rigorous experimental field ecology while addressing fundamental questions about population dynamics, species interactions, and trophic cascades. The student will be closely involved in designing and implementing experiments, collecting and managing field data, analyzing results, and communicating findings through scientific presentations and publications.

The ability to work both independently and collaboratively as part of a research team.
Strong organizational and data-management skills.
Good scientific writing and communication skills.
A strong work ethic and enthusiasm for intensive field-based research.

This position is particularly well suited for someone who wants to develop as an independent field ecologist and gain experience conducting a manipulative ecological experiment from field implementation through analysis and publication.

Description
A two-year postdoctoral fellowship is available with Dr. Mitch Weegman in the Department of Biology at the University of Saskatchewan (https://www.ducks.ca/our-work/science/saskatchewan-endowed-chair/), in collaboration with Drs. Todd Arnold (Delta Waterfowl Foundation) and Matt Dyson (Ducks Unlimited Canada). The postdoctoral fellow will lead a research project estimating the population dynamics of North American ducks and their environmental drivers, using 65-year data sets to address long-standing questions about synchrony in multispecies demographic rates as well as the impact of agricultural intensity (e.g., pesticide application rates in the Canadian prairies) and cross-seasonal effects on duck reproductive success, survival, and population structure. This work extends substantial ecological and statistical developments on duck population dynamics led by the late Dr. Dan Gibson (University of Minnesota/University of Saskatchewan).
 Our team has focused on estimating the effects of habitat and harvest management on demographic rates in northern pintails, using an integrated metapopulation model to link pintail demography within and among breeding and wintering regions. We anticipate expanding this model to multiple dabbling and diving duck species for greater ecological perspective and conservation utility. We also anticipate exploring linkages between demographic rates and pesticide, insecticide and fungicide application rates across the Canadian prairies, for fuller context about relationships between agricultural intensification and duck reproductive success. There will be opportunities to explore related research questions and collaborate on several projects in movement and population ecology in the Weegman lab, as well as with Delta Waterfowl Foundation and Ducks Unlimited Canada.
 Prerequisites: Ideal candidates will have a PhD in ecology, statistics or a closely related field, and interpersonal skills to lead discussions among collaborators. Preference will be given to those with a strong quantitative background (e.g., experience with Program R, Bayesian methods) and knowledge of migratory bird ecology and management. Students must have a valid driver’s license. The successful applicant will be expected to publish manuscripts in peer-reviewed journals and present papers at scientific meetings.

Dr. Lisa Izzo (Fisheries and Aquatic Conservation Ecology Lab) in the School of Natural Resources at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville is seeking applicants for a M.S. student in Wildlife and Fisheries Science. The student’s thesis work will focus on understanding movements of adult lake sturgeon in the Tennessee River using acoustic telemetry, with a particular emphasis on locating potential spawning areas and documenting successful spawning via egg and/or larval drift sampling. This collaborative project will give the student the opportunity to work closely with project partners including the Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency (TWRA), Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), and others. 
 Duties: In addition to course requirements of the M.S. in Wildlife and Fisheries Science program, primary duties of the student will include (1) surgical tagging and active tracking of adult lake sturgeon; (2) maintenance of a stationary acoustic receiver array; (3) study design and deployment of various gears to sample sturgeon eggs and larvae; (4) data management and analysis; (5) presentations to project partners and at regional/national conferences; and (6) writing of a final thesis, at least one manuscript for submission to a peer-reviewed journal, and reports to project funders. The selected applicant will have the opportunity to develop and investigate hypotheses and address objectives of interest within the context of the project. Field work will take place at large river/reservoir sites, so trailering, launching, driving, and working on boats is required. Field work may take place at irregular hours, especially larval sampling.   
 Location: The position will be based at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. 
 Start Date: November 1, 2026 preferred, January 2027 at the latest (Contingent on funding timeline) 
 Qualifications: Successful applicants must have a Bachelor’s degree in Natural Resources, Ecology, Wildlife Science/Management, Fisheries Science/Management, or a closely related field, and meet all other qualifications for admission to the School of Natural Resources Master’s Program (https://naturalresources.tennessee.edu/masters-program/). Please note that GRE scores are optional for admission. Applicants should have an interest in aquatic research and fisheries management, and a strong desire to learn new skills through the graduate school process. The successful candidate must possess a valid driver’s license and be able to lead field work independently. Prior experience in aquatic field work (particularly on boats), minor boat maintenance, acoustic telemetry equipment, and/or data analysis and management in statistical software is preferred but not required. 
 Salary and Benefits: $37,000/year stipend for 3 years, coverage for tuition, and health insurance benefits. The student will be responsible for paying graduate student fees. 
 To Apply: Please email (1) a one-page statement of research interests and career goals, (2) a CV, (3) unofficial transcripts, and (4) contact information for three references to Dr. Lisa Izzo (lizzo1@utk.edu) with a subject line of MS Application Lake Sturgeon and your last name. Applications are due September 7th and review will begin immediately after. Successful candidate will apply formally to the UTK graduate school following the internal application process.
Contact
Lisa Izzo
lizzo1@utk.edu (preferred contact method)

Postdoc Summary:
The Wildlife and Water Lab (WWL), based at the Odum School of
Ecology, University of Georgia (UGA), Athens, invites applications for a postdoctoral
candidate in Spatial Biodiversity Data and Conservation Applications beginning January 15,
2027 (or earlier if possible). The position is 2-year (24 months) non-tenure track
appointment, and the salary is competitive and commensurate with qualifications and
experience. The successful candidate will conduct quantitative analyses of the
ecohydrology of terrestrial birds and participate in an ongoing, multi-institution project
developing frameworks and support tools for measuring the biodiversity enhancement
(i.e., net gain) of projects under the IUCN Global Standard for Nature-based Solutions’
Criterion 3.

Responsibilities: 
The postdoctoral associate will work under the mentorship of Dr.
Charles van Rees (Odum School of Ecology) and in collaboration with graduate students
in the WWL and other faculty at UGA on (1) spatial ecological research on the
relationship between terrestrial birds, wetlands, and riparian habitats, and (2)
biodiversity accounting for Nature-based Solutions projects. Specific responsibilities
include (a) accessing, processing, managing, and analyzing large datasets including
river flow data, remote sensing imagery, and spatially explicit biodiversity data (e.g.,
eBird, NEON), (b) testing ecological hypotheses through quantitative spatial analysis,
including via machine learning and Bayesian approaches, (c) developing browser-based
decision-making tools from existing frameworks and publicly available datasets, and (d)
leveraging and training Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents to support decision-making tool

Description
Our Sea Turtle Life Support and Water Quality Internship offers college students and recent graduates a unique, hands-on opportunity to gain experience in water quality management and in maintaining life support systems for aquatic animal care. Interns work under the guidance of KBSTRRC’s Life Support Systems Coordinator, contributing directly to the daily operations of our sea turtle hospital and the care of our patients.
Free Housing! Free, shared housing with utilities included is provided. Our intern guest house is conveniently located next door to our sea turtle hospital. Housing is co-ed, and interns will have their own room but should expect to share a bathroom with one other intern of the same gender. No pets are allowed. Living on-site is optional during the non-summer semesters. 
Stipend Available! Full-time or part-time hours available. Interns should expect to pay for food, travel to and from the internship, entertainment and recreation, and any other personal expenses which are not part of the internship. If interns choose to live off-site, they are responsible for housing costs. 
School Credit: School credit may be available from your institution. The intern is responsible for completing all paperwork and paying all fees required by their institution to receive credit for their internship.
Duration: The Life Support and Water Quality Internship runs for 12-18 weeks. The start date is flexible within October or November. Interns should expect an irregular work schedule consisting of weekdays, weekends, and holidays. Some workdays may exceed eight hours.

As the Natural Resource Scientist 1 for the Center for Sustaining Agriculture and Natural Resources, you carry out specific and limited research objectives focused on issues affecting food‑energy‑water systems in the Pacific Northwest within the agricultural and natural resources domain. Description
 Postdoctoral Position: Parasite/Pathogen Evolution, Ecology, and Spillover 
 Department: Department of Fish and Wildlife Conservation, Virginia Tech
 
 Appointment: Full-time, one-year postdoctoral appointment (renewable)
 
 Location: Blacksburg, Virginia, with potential travel for project meetings and stakeholder engagement
 
 Position summary: The Department of Fish and Wildlife Conservation at Virginia Tech invites applications for a postdoctoral research associate to study the evolutionary, ecological, and landscape-level drivers of viral and/or parasite diversity, zoonotic spillover, and bioinformatics. The postdoctoral researcher will integrate viral/parasite and host phylogenies, environmental data, spatial epidemiology, and laboratory-generated viral sequence data to test an expanded spillover framework that explicitly incorporates secondary hosts, environmental conditions, host switching, viral/parasite diversification, and human disease outcomes. This position is well suited to a scientist with strong experience in disease ecology, evolution, comparative phylogenetics, bioinformatics, molecular epidemiology, or a closely related field who is interested in interdisciplinary, reproducible research with public-health relevance. 
 Research responsibilities: The successful candidate will study host relatedness, environmental conditions, viral diversification, host range evolution, virulence, or population dynamics. The investigator will implement and extend evolutionary models to evaluate host switching, phylogenetic conservatism, population structure, fronts of spread, gene expression or host-virus/parasite coevolution. It is expected that the successful applicant will integrate viral/parasite genomic data with host occurrence, host community data, climate, land-cover, and other environmental datasets from NEON, GBIF, WorldClim, GenBank, and related sources. The postdoc will mentor graduate and undergraduate researchers and contribute to project training workshops and stakeholder engagement activities. The postdoc will prepare manuscripts, conference presentations, reports, and grant-related products. They will also develop reproducible and well-documented computational workflows for data cleaning, sequence processing, phylogenetic inference, statistical modeling, visualization, and data management. 
 Required qualifications 
Ph.D. in ecology, evolutionary biology, disease ecology, bioinformatics, or a closely related discipline by the start date.
Demonstrated research experience in at least two of the following areas: pathogen or disease ecology; viral evolution; molecular epidemiology; comparative phylogenetics; bioinformatics; evolutionary modeling, spatial epidemiology; population dynamics; or ecological modeling.
Strong programming and statistical-analysis skills in R (and/or other relevant programming languages like Julia) including data manipulation, visualization, and model development.
Experience working with biological sequence data and phylogenetic analyses.
Ability to design, execute, document, and troubleshoot independent research workflows.
Experience analyzing complex, heterogeneous datasets and integrating data from multiple sources.
Demonstrated ability to communicate research effectively through peer-reviewed publications, presentations, and collaborative work.
Ability to work productively in an interdisciplinary team and to mentor junior researchers.
Commitment to safe, ethical, and reproducible research practices, including compliance with applicable biosafety, animal-use, data-use, and institutional requirements.

 

Preferred qualifications
 Experience with RevBayes, BEAST, MrBayes, IQ-TREE, or other Bayesian or maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tools.
Experience with developing novel macroevolutionary models.
Experience with viral phylogenetics, RNA viruses, segmented viral genomes, phylodynamics, ancestral-state reconstruction, or host- parasite coevolutionary models.
Experience with molecular virology or pathogen diagnostics, including RNA extraction, PCR/qPCR, amplicon generation, library preparation, or next-generation sequencing.
Experience with spatial statistics, hierarchical or generalized linear models, occupancy or prevalence modeling, time-series analysis, or landscape epidemiology.
Familiarity with ecological niche modeling and environmental or species-distribution data, including WorldClim, GBIF, NEON, or similar resources.
Experience using Git/GitHub, Unix/Linux, high-performance computing, workflow managers, containers, or other tools for reproducible computational research.
Programming experience in Python, Bash, or another scientific programming language.
Experience managing, curating, and documenting large genomic or ecological datasets.
Familiarity with GIS software or geospatial analysis in R.
Record of publishing interdisciplinary research and/or obtaining research funding.
Experience communicating science to nonacademic audiences.

 

Professional Development: The postdoctoral researcher will have opportunities to develop an independent research profile while contributing to the project’s broader impacts. Activities may include coauthoring manuscripts, presenting at scientific meetings, mentoring students, helping deliver online training workshops, participating in stakeholder workshops, and contributing to public-health and disease-prevention communications. The postdoctoral researcher will have the opportunity to join professional programs at Virginia Tech such as the Global Change Center (GCC) and the Center for Emerging, Zoonotic, and Arthropod-borne Pathogens (CeZAP) under the guidance of Dr. Luis Escobar.The position also supports professional development in grant writing, project management, open and reproducible science, interdisciplinary collaboration, and international research translation.
 
 

Work environment: The researcher will join an interdisciplinary team in disease ecology, conservation biology, evolutionary biology, quantitative modeling, and molecular epidemiology composed of one PI, two CoPIs, four PhD students, one visiting professor, and one postdoc. Occasional travel may be required for project meetings, workshops, conferences, or stakeholder engagement.
 
 

Application materials: Applicants should submit their documents to Dr. Luis Escobar (escobar1@vt.edu) in a single PDF including an updated curriculum vitae, 2-page cover letter describing research experience and interest in the project, up to one page statement describing relevant computational, phylogenetic, laboratory, or disease-ecology experience, contact information for three professional references, and up to three representative publications or preprints. Candidates with strengths in either computational/evolutionary analysis or molecular epidemiology are encouraged to apply.

 

Application deadline: August 30, 2026. 5:00 pm



Anticipated start date: January 9, 2027, or earlier.



Salary and benefits: $60,000, in addition to applicable fringe benefits and health insurance in accordance with university policies



Virginia Tech is an equal opportunity employer. The university welcomes applications from candidates whose backgrounds and experiences will contribute to an inclusive research and training environment.

Luis E Escobar

Description
Title- Puget Sound Sampling Unit Biologist
Classification- Fish & Wildlife Biologist 3
Job Status- Full-Time / Permanent
WDFW Program- Fish Program – Puget Sound Management
Duty Station- Olympia, Washington – Thurston County
Hybrid/Telework-  This position may include telework options at the discretion of the supervisor. 

Learn more about being a member of Team WDFW! 


As a senior-level biologist, you will supervise and oversee the collection of dockside recreational and commercial fisheries data across the Puget Sound and the Strait of Juan de Fuca, Marine Areas 5 through 13.

Working closely with the Puget Sound Sampling Unit Manager, play a key role in the planning and developing of biological research and coordinating data collection to support stock assessment and fisheries management. 


What to Expect:
Among the varied range of responsibilities held within this role, the Puget Sound Sampling Unit Biologist will, 

Supervise Puget Sound Sampling Unit (PSSU) Dockside Fisheries Sampling Operations: 
Directly supervise creel and biological data collection conducted dockside for recreational and commercial fisheries in Marine Areas 5 through 13.
Provide technical guidance to field supervisors on biological sampling problems and issues to ensure compliance with established sampling methods, techniques, and plans.
Coordinate seasonal and weekly fisheries sampling schedules, including halibut and summer and winter salmon fisheries.
Coordinate sampling efforts within and across geographic areas in the unit to ensure consistent and complete fisheries sampling activities.
Develop, implement, and oversee employee training and onboarding processes for dockside sampling positions.
Coordinate with Sampler Support staff to ensure field staff have access to programs and systems needed for biological data collection and administrative processes, including iForms, SharePoint, Microsoft Teams, TotalTime, Outlook, and TEMS.
Review and approve administrative paperwork submitted by field supervisors and their staff, including timesheets, travel vouchers, p-card logs, Order Payment Forms, personal reimbursements, and other purchasing documents.
Provide field supervisors with resources, training, and professional development opportunities to strengthen technical, supervisory, and leadership skills.
Coordinate and assist field supervisors with hiring, training, and evaluation of dockside sampling staff across South Sound (Olympia), the Peninsula (Port Angeles), North Sound (Bellingham) and Central Sound (Edmonds).
Provide timely, confidential, and professional guidance on personnel issues and seek assistance from supervisor, chain of command, or Human Resources as appropriate.

Coordinate Human Resources (HR) Activities for Dockside Sampling Positions:
Serve as the primary coordinator for HR activities affecting dockside sampling positions, including position descriptions, recruitments, HR actions, appointments, separations, promotions, reallocations, and organizational changes.
Track staffing needs, personnel actions, appointment timelines, and recruitment activities to ensure adequate staffing for fisheries sampling operations.
Review and coordinate HR documents and processes for accuracy, completeness, and compliance with established requirements and timelines.
Maintain current personnel records, staffing spreadsheets, organizational charts, and other workforce information.
Provide guidance to field supervisors and staff on HR and payroll policies, processes, systems, forms, and timelines, including online HR processes through the HR Service Portal.
Coordinate regularly with HR Recruitment, HR Operations, and HR Data Team and advise the Puget Sound Sampling Unit Manager on staffing and HR-related issues.

Ensure Quality and Completion of Fisheries Data and Documentation:
Oversee the timely review, editing, and quality control of recreational dockside fisheries data in coordination with PSSU data manager in the unit’s online portal.
Develop, review, and implement fisheries sampling protocols, procedures, and sampling goals in coordination with unit staff and tribal biologists.
Evaluate fisheries data and assist with developing procedures and approaches to meet program sampling needs.
Support fisheries studies and special data collection projects, including planning, study design, and coordination with data managers.
Oversee tracking and maintenance of electronic data collection equipment and related systems.
Create, review, and edit fisheries-related manuals, protocols, reports, spreadsheets, and other technical documentation.

Coordinate Fisheries Sampling, Training, and Technical Support:
Coordinate fisheries sampling activities with staff and external partners to support comprehensive recreational and commercial fisheries data collection (tribal and non-tribal) for Puget Sound.
Coordinate field-based training with field supervisors and provide technical support to ensure consistent sampling methods, data collection procedures, and documentation.
Collaborate with Fish Program staff to develop training objectives, materials, and techniques for biological sampling activities.
Evaluate sampling procedures, equipment use, data collection methods, and electronic data forms to identify opportunities for improvement.
Communicate data quality concerns and recommend improvements to sampling procedures, training, and logistics.
Conduct dockside sampling for salmon, halibut, marine fish, shrimp, crab, and other fisheries as needed.


Working Conditions:

Work Setting, including hazards:
Work is primarily in an office setting (90%). Fieldwork is conducted in varying weather and sea conditions. Fieldwork involves exposure to noise, odors, repetitive movements of hands, finger manipulations, long periods of sitting, squatting, walking, boating for angler interviews, climbing in and out of boats, sampling salmon in a boat, carrying, kneeling, rarely heavy lifting (up to 40 pounds unassisted) containers of fish, working and standing in confined space, fish blood and slime, slippery surfaces, biting and stinging insects, use of knives, transporting agency staff and equipment in agency vehicles. This position may involve working in or near water, including tasks that require navigating, negotiating, and performing duties related to water environments.

Schedule:
24/7 non-scheduled with weekends and evenings required. Workdays are typically 8 to 10 hours and may occur between 5:00 a.m. and 11:00 p.m.

Travel Requirements:
Travel throughout the Puget Sound area, with regular overnight travel required.

Tools and Equipment:
iPad, electronic sampling equipment (CWT detector), weighing scale, calculator, knives, forceps, head lamp, measuring board, tally counter, tide book, totes/bins, paper forms, labels, scale cards, pencils, pens, clipboard, scissors, personal flotation device (PFD), WDFW apparel, gloves, rain gear, and current recreational and commercial sampling manuals.

Customer Interactions:
Interact with WDFW and Tribal staff, commercial harvester and fishers, salmon buyers, fish processors, recreational anglers, shellfishers, and the public. Provide basic information regarding fisheries resources, agency programs and activities, and sport fishing regulations. Interactions may include contact with individuals who are upset or frustrated. Serve as a liaison with the regional supervisor and enforcement staff regarding fishery violations observed in the field.


Qualifications:

Required Qualifications:

Option 1:
Two (2) years as a Fish & Wildlife Biologist 2. 

Option 2 – All of the following:
A Bachelor's degree in fisheries, wildlife management, natural resource science, environmental science, or closely related field.
Three (3) years of professional experience in fish management or fish research, wildlife management or wildlife research, or habitat management or habitat research. 

Option 3 – All of the following:
A Master’s degree in fisheries, wildlife management, natural resource science, environmental science, or closely related field.
Two (2) years of professional experience in fish management or fish research, wildlife management or wildlife research, or habitat management or habitat research. 

Option 4 – All of the following:
A Doctorate’s degree in fisheries, wildlife management, natural resource science, environmental science, or closely related field.
One (1) year of professional experience in fish management or fish research, wildlife management or wildlife research, or habitat management or habitat research. 

Option 5:
Seven (7) years of professional experience in fish management or fish research, wildlife management or wildlife research, or habitat management or habitat research. 

For the options above, the following experience is also required and may be gained concurrently:
Two (2) years of supervisory experience.
Advanced proficiency with computer software applications, including Microsoft Access, Excel, Word, and PowerPoint.

Certifications/Licenses:
Valid driver’s license.


Preferred Qualifications:
In addition to the required qualifications, our ideal applicant will possess one or more of the following:
Master’s Degree or higher in fisheries, wildlife management, natural resource science, or environmental science, or a closely related field.
Twelve (12) months of experience conducting creel surveys and/or sampling sport and/or commercial fisheries.
Ability to identify salmon, marine fish, and shellfish fish species found in Puget Sound.  
Knowledge of salmon life history, Puget Sound sport fishing regulations, and commercial and sport fishing methods and gear.
Familiarity with WDFW administrative, human resources, and payroll procedures and policies.
Strong organizational and time management skills.

 
Your application should include the following:
A completed online application showcasing how your qualifications align with the job requirements.
An up-to-date resume.
A cover letter detailing your interest in the position, your relevant skills and experience, and why you are the ideal candidate.
At least three (3) professional references with current contact information.

Title- Hatchery Data Steward
Classification- Fish & Wildlife Biologist 3
Job Status- Full-Time/Permanent
WDFW Program- Fish Program – Hatchery Data Unit
Duty Station- Olympia, Washington – Thurston County
Hybrid/Telework- The selected candidate may be able to telework/work remotely up to four (4) days per week at the discretion of the supervisor.

Learn more about being a member of Team WDFW!


In this senior-level biologist position, you will plan and develop resource management assessments and provide results that have direct impact on key program decisions.

As part of the Hatchery Data Section team, your work will contribute to the mission of enumerating and replicating the most accurate and complete set of information, and to disseminate and share inclusively and easily.

Collaborate with colleagues within the agency and coordinate with external entities and organizations while preparing, assessing, and interpreting hatchery fish resource information.


What to Expect-
Among the varied range of responsibilities held within this role, the Hatchery Data Steward will,

Administer the Future Brood Document for multi-agency hatchery production planning purposes:
Function as the agency’s technical coordinator for the Equilibrium Brood/Future Brood program under the US v. Washington and US v. Oregon federal court agreements for state-wide hatchery production.
Coordinate for co-managers, including 24 tribes and multiple federal agencies, in the development of the Future Brood Document/Equilibrium Brood Document (FBD) under the Puget Sound Management Agreement.
Prepare, assess, and interpret the resource management planning document that guides production across all state, tribal, and federal facilities.
Manage, compile, and distribute this document to fulfill agency compliance with co-managers under the Puget Sound Management Plan (PSMP), which has a direct impact on key hatchery program decisions and operations. 
Facilitate discussions as needed to ensure compliance with Hatchery Genetic Management Plans, Fish Disease Control Policy, and legal mandates and requirements under the PSMP.
Conduct annual Regional Review Meetings with internal and external staff.

Support Regional Fisheries Enhancement Groups (RFEG) with hatchery carcass duties and serve as the Hatchery Data Steward:
Perform accounting and hatchery operational activities such as carcass data entry, carcass reports, invoice billing, and other reports in support of RFEG. 
Collect, review, and compile hatchery data to ensure accurate, thorough, efficient, and meaningful capture of hatchery information for managers and outside entities to make decisions regarding fisheries.
Oversee Hatchery Ticket (Form 3) data entry including reviewing for accuracy, comparing to FishBooks, and ensuring safe and secure storage of information.
Conduct advanced evaluation and analysis of hatchery adult data; analyze information for completeness and accuracy and formulate conclusions.
Reconcile hatchery coded wire tag (CWT) data with the tag lab.
Participate and provide expertise in RFEG process and meetings as needed; provide analytical expertise, information, and assistance in developing contracts for surplus carcass and eggs.

Serve as the statewide staff expert on the FishBooks hatchery management database:
Coordinate and lead state-wide training sessions to staff including managers, biologists, and hatchery workers.
Provide technical support for database users including corrections, missing options, and system errors.

Hatchery reporting:
Assess and interpret hatchery data to produce professional reports that are an accurate reflection of hatchery information and meet the requirements of the agency.
Provide information summaries to managers, scientists, government officials, and fishery entities for use in making fisheries management, production, and fiscal decisions.
 

Working Conditions:

Work Setting, including hazards: Work is primarily performed in an office environment. Occasional fieldwork may be performed in all weather conditions and may require performing strenuous physical activities, such as repetitively handling fish and lifting fish feed (weighing at least 50 pounds). This position may involve working in or near water, including tasks that require navigating, negotiating, and performing duties related to water environments.

Schedule: Typically, Monday – Friday, averaging 40 hours per week. The standard work schedule includes the potential for occasional evening or weekend work as needed. Alternative schedules may be considered based on business needs

Travel Requirements: Occasionally travel to agency locations for meetings and other business needs.

Tools and Equipment: Hatchery tools may include spawning knives, Zephyr gun, measuring boards, dip nets, seine nets, and buckets.

Customer Interactions: Regularly interact with hatchery personnel throughout the state to provide technical assistance, answer questions, and assist with various tasks.


Qualifications:

Closely related qualifying experience may be substituted for the required education on a year-by-year basis.

Required Qualifications:

Option 1, all of the following: 
A Bachelor’s degree in fisheries, wildlife management, environmental science, natural resources science, or a related field.
Three (3) years of professional experience in fish management or research, wildlife management or research, or habitat management or research.
Valid Driver’s License.

Option 2, all of the following:
Two (2) years as a Fish & Wildlife Biologist 2.
Valid Driver’s License.

For either option listed above, experience with all of the following is required:
Experience may be gained concurrently.
Fisheries, hatchery operations, aquatic biology, or related biological program support.
Fish biology, hatchery production systems, and fisheries management principles.
Applying biological sampling methods, data interpretation, and basic statistical concepts in applied fisheries or aquaculture settings.
Managing, entering, validating, and maintaining a high volume of biological or fisheries datasets in structured databases such as FishBooks, Access, or SQL-based systems.
Performing accurate high-volume data entry and maintaining data integrity.
Providing customer service, technical assistance, or support to internal or external customers.
Ability to communicate effectively, both verbally and in writing, and work collaboratively with a variety of staff and stakeholders.

Please note:
A Master’s degree in the applicable field of study may substitute for one (1) year of the required professional experience in fish management or research, wildlife management or research, or habitat management or research.
A PhD in the applicable field of study may substitute for two (2) years of the required professional experience in fish management or research, wildlife management or research, or habitat management or research.
 

Preferred Qualifications:
In addition to the required qualifications, our ideal applicant will possess some or all the following:

Experience in/with:
More than three (3) years of hatchery experience, including experience with multiple species, life stages, hatchery programs, production planning, or hatchery management functions.
Microsoft Access including database design, query development, report generation, data relationships, and troubleshooting database issues.
Analyzing large fisheries or hatchery datasets to identify trends, improve data quality, and support management decisions.
SQL and database querying.
Providing technical support, training, or customer service to database users, including developing guidance documents, training materials, or standard operating procedures.
FishBooks, Regional Mark Information System (RMIS), coded wire tag (CWT) databases, or other fisheries and hatchery information systems.
Participating in database development, user acceptance testing, business process improvement, or implementation of new software applications.

Competencies:
Advanced proficiency in Microsoft Excel, including complex formulas, PivotTables, charts, dashboards, data validation, and automated reporting tools.
Knowledge of hatchery production reporting requirements, broodstock management, fish health tracking, fish marking/tagging programs, or release processes.
Demonstrated ability to independently identify operational issues, develop solutions, and collaborate with hatchery staff, biologists, and information technology personnel to improve data systems and business processes.
 

Your application must include the following:
A completed online application showcasing how your qualifications align with the job requirements.
An up-to-date resume.
A cover letter detailing your interest in the position, your relevant skills and experience, and why you are the ideal candidate.
At least three professional references with current contact information.

The Wildlife Ecology and Land Management Lab at the University of Florida is seeking a Field Research Technician to assist with multiple research projects focused on wildlife habitat management and longleaf pine ecosystem restoration in the Florida Panhandle.

The technician will primarily assist with deploying and maintaining camera trap arrays used to monitor wildlife communities across restoration and management sites. Responsibilities will also include organizing and identifying wildlife in camera trap images to support ongoing research and data management. In addition, the technician will conduct vegetation surveys to quantify habitat characteristics associated with wildlife use and restoration outcomes. These projects aim to improve understanding of how wildlife communities respond to habitat management and longleaf pine restoration, providing valuable data to inform conservation and land management decisions.

Organizing and reviewing camera trap imagery

Bachelor of Science degree in wildlife biology, ecology, natural resources, or a closely related field

Experience navigating using GPS and driving in 4-wheel drive conditions

Description
 PROJECT MANAGER (Consultant) 

North American Summit on Collaborating with Wildlife 


The Project Manager for the North American Summit on Collaborating with Wildlife (CW Summit) is a vital part of the Wildlife Restoration Foundation (WRF) leadership team, working directly with the WRF President and Directors of Operations, Programs, and Marketing to maximize results in terms of registrations, content, funds raised, operational efficiency, and new partnerships. The CW Summit is a project of the WRF Collaborating with Wildlife Program which focuses on meeting the needs of native wildlife in North America as human communities expand across and impact essential habitats on land and in freshwater and marine environments. 

The CW Summit is a large-scale, multi-sector professional convening designed as a milepost in the long game of ensuring human actions provision for, support, adapt to, and value native wildlife, particularly as human development occurs around or trammels habitat neighboring protected areas. Hosted by WRF and the Oceans & Wildlife Institute (OWI), the CW Summit is taking place at the Hilliard Center in Corpus Christi, Texas on February 2-4, 2027, with an OWI field trip to the Port of Corpus Christi Wildlife Rescue Operations Center on February 5. 

The Summit is not a conference but uses a process of exploring Models & Methodologies (M&Ms) of “Collaborating with Wildlife,” a term that we and our partners have coined to recognize and address native wildlife needs, in advance. Our team is identifying and soliciting M&Ms from across many sectors of human endeavor—conservation, government, Tribes/First Nations, ranching, farming, zoos and aquariums, engineering, construction, transportation, and more—then engaging experienced practitioners and researchers to present their M&Ms in Workgroup Dialogues at the Summit. In the Workgroups, dialogists will discover CW best practices that can be replicated or adapted in multiple places and species. Panel Dialogues with full-group participation will strive to diagnose the innovations needed to overcome barriers to M&M implementation and identify resources and new partners that ensure success. The Summit aims to enrich the more technical content with special features—historical accounts, photography and film, art, language, and cultural expressions that inspire humans to meet wildlife needs so that four pillars of human action (Supporting, Provisioning, Adapting, and Valuing) bolster native wildlife populations and assure they can thrive in a common pursuit of ecological regeneration. 

The successful candidate for the CW Summit Project Manager (PM) position will be able to understand and make a strong case for Collaborating with Wildlife to any potential participant, no matter the sector. In addition: 

·       The first task of the PM will be able to produce a strategic plan for meeting the registrations goal and serve in a CWS chief of staff role to ensure all WRF team members working on the Summit are engaged, productive, and valued. Once approved, the strategic plan will be the guiding document for measuring PM performance. Detailed strategic plan elements to be managed by the PM will be shared with each candidate as Key Position Responsibilities after an initial screening interview. 

·       The primary goal of the position is to maximize Summit registrations (minimum of 300 by December 1, 2026), managing CW Summit (CWS) subteams toward this measurable outcome. 

·       The PM will manage CWS subteams, labeled Programming, Operations/Logistics, Fundraising, Marketing & Communications, and Onsite. Within some of these subteams are existing coordinators that have internal teams of their own (e.g., Vendors, Exhibitors & Silent Auction or Zoo & Aquarium Training Track). 

The CW Project Manager will be a consultant to WRF and paid a monthly stipend based on measured productivity. The consultant should be regularly available during the hours of 9:00a-5:00p Eastern time and can work remotely, except for during the Summit itself, which requires being on-site to lead/help meet Summit and facility-related needs from January 30 through February 5, 2027. The period of this consultancy is September 1, 2026 to February 28, 2027, engaged under a written consultancy agreement where the PM is expected to work an average of 24-32 hours per week. This PM role is intended for a highly competent, reliable and personable professional with experience, confidence, and self-motivation and exceptional degree of productivity found amongst others on the WRF leadership team and meet both goals of the PM position without prompting as committed also to the mission of the WRF Collaborating with Wildlife Program itself. 


Education & Experience: 

●     Bachelor’s degree at a minimum; Master’s or graduate work in related subject ideal 

●     At least 2–3 years of experience planning and executing large-scale events, conferences, or multi-day programs 

●     Strong organizational and time management skills, with demonstrated ability to manage multiple concurrent workstreams and deadlines and to work independently and proactively, and always responsive to the Exec Team 

●     Excellent communication and interpersonal abilities, with proven aptitude for managing teams well 

●     Proficiency in event management software and tools; experience with Whova, Wix, Slack, Mailchimp, and Google Workspace preferred 

●     Experience developing and tracking event budgets and financial reporting 

●     Demonstrated commitment to working with a nonprofit, mission-driven organization 

●     Passion for wildlife and the meeting of their needs, with experience working with parks and gateway communities a plus 

 

To apply: Send a short (less than one page) cover letter, a resume with 2 references to info@wildlifeandparks.org. Please name the electronic file sent in this format: [MMDDYY]_CWSProgramManager_ [Your Name]. Be sure to put your name and words “CWS Program Manager Candidate” in the subject line of your email. Please follow these instructions closely. 

Thank you for your interest in working with the Wildlife Restoration Foundation team and our mission to recover and protect North America’s wildlife!

Description
 Title: Bobcat Project Technicians in Colorado 

Agency: Colorado Parks and Wildlife 

Location: near Meeker Colorado and then near Deckers, Colorado 

Salary: $19.29/hour 

Start Date: Four field technician positions to start 10/12/2026 

End Date: late March 2027 

Last Date to apply: 08/30/2026 at 11:59 

JOB DESCRIPTION: Colorado Parks and Wildlife (CPW) is seeking seasonal fieldworkers for late fall and winter work on a mesocarnivore—bobcats (Lynx rufus). These are ~6-month positions stationed near Deckers, Colorado. The late fall work (October) consists of (I) maintaining camera traps in two 400 square kilometer study areas, (II) surveying leporid pellet plots near the cameras, and (III) the primary work consists of live capturing and collaring of bobcats (Lynx rufus) over the winter (November-March). 

In addition to these tasks, other secondary duties will be assigned, such as bait collection, helping other CPW personnel within the study areas, photo ID, and more. 

During the fall/winter capture work, fieldworkers will typically work in 2-3 person teams, one for each study area, and will often be required to work alone and independently. Shared housing will be provided and you might be required to share a room. 

There is substantial driving on less-than-ideal road/trail conditions and basic vehicle care and maintenance is part of routine. Keeping vehicles clean is part of that maintenance. State or rental vehicles, UTVs, snowmobiles (if required), housing, and fuel for work are provided. Internet is also available and provided, but speed varies, and is prioritized for work use. Work and living conditions can be socially isolating with the exception of nearby coworkers. Recreational opportunities are certainly available in the area during off time. 

Schedules vary, but are usually 5 days on and 2 days off. Everyone has the ~same schedule during training, but is staggered during captures. Crew leads determine schedules that best fit with field conditions and project requirements. 

Teams are largely independent, but the project lead makes monthly visits, is on-call for assistance, conducts regular meetings, and helps triage and pivot as issues might arise in the field. 

DURATION OF EMPLOYMENT: 
 --- 10/12/2026 – 03/26/2027 (4 positions) --- 

QUALIFICATIONS: Applicants must be in good physical condition and work well with others. Applicants are preferred to have graduated from or enrolled in a wildlife/natural resource university program, but this is not required. Fieldwork and seasons involving wildlife is a must. Applicants must be able to hike up to 1-2 miles per day in rugged, sometimes loose, rocky terrain, while carrying 20-30 lbs (e.g. live traps) and hike longer distances, or ~6-10 miles/day with lighter weight (e.g. 15 lbs or several camera traps). Applicants must be able to handle and transport animal carcasses used for bait. Applicants must be diligent and accurate when collecting and entering data. Applicants must possess a valid driver’s license and demonstrate backcountry (GPS/compass) navigational skills. Applicants must be able to live and work effectively, peaceably, and patiently in close quarters with other technicians under field conditions. Applicants must be good communicators, critical thinkers, and also follow project protocols and set priorities. Good communication means being respectful and also aware and sometimes anticipatory of people’s and project needs. Project priorities might change based on varying field conditions or unforeseen challenges, which also requires flexibility and acceptance on part of the applicant. 
 Basic requirements are (1) having had at least two field seasons of wildlife work for ≥3 month duration each, (2) live capture and animal handling experience, (3) 4x4 driving, OHV proficiency and trailering, (4) attention to detail and ability to follow detailed data collection protocols, and (5) being of good and amiable character. 
 In addition to the above, candidates who (6) have experience with chemical immobilization of animals or live captures of carnivores, (7) basic mechanical skills, (8) climbing experience, (9) have had regular contact with landowners or recreationists while working, (10) have had winter fieldwork in snowy conditions, and those who (11) have successfully lived AND worked with colleagues for >3 months in field conditions will be preferred. 
 Even if you do not have all of these preferred skills, I still encourage you to apply, as the candidate pool can vary substantially and teams can have a variety of skillsets among its members. 
 Candidates must be willing to undergo a background check. In your RESUME or CV, specifically mention your experience/ability in each of the qualifications mentioned in this announcement. 
 HOW TO APPLY: 
(1) fill out the google form application in full (link below) and 
(2) upload RESUME or CV, including 3 PROFESSIONAL references by 08/30/2026 11:59 PM (MDT) to the… 
(3) cover letters are not required and will not be screened unless already selected for an interview; the application (below google link) gives you the opportunity to highlight things about yourself in hopefully a quick, efficient way. 
 Bobcat Field Work Application 2026-2027 link: 
https://forms.gle/Sr2dqNT5KV72yKWJA
 All uploaded forms must have the following format: 
{yourLASTname}_{yourFIRSTname}_CV_bobcat_applicant_2026-2027 
 Example file name: “Frank_Shane_CV_bobcat_applicant_2026-2027” 
 If references are uploaded separately from the CV, replace “CV” in file name with “REF” for that file alone. 
 If you require or desire further information, please contact Colorado Parks and Wildlife Researcher  Dr. Shane Frank at shane.frank@state.co.us. 
Contact
Shane Frank
shane.frank@state.co.us (preferred contact method)

Description

The Chintimini Wildlife Center 

The Chintimini Wildlife Center provides care for injured and orphaned wildlife with the goal of returning them to their natural habitat, and fosters a connection between people and wildlife through education. Chintimini is home to a wildlife rehabilitation clinic as well as an extensive education program – all located right outside Corvallis, Oregon. 

Wildlife Rehabilitation Specialist 

The Wildlife Rehabilitation Specialist will work with the Wildlife Rehabilitation Team to provide care to rehabilitation patients in our clinic. The specialist is responsible for performing the triage, initial treatment, and continuing care for sick, orphaned, and injured wildlife. The specialist works under the direction of the Wildlife Rehabilitation Program Director to follow procedures for rehabilitating animals. 

This position works in cooperation with other rehabilitation staff, interns, and volunteers to provide quality care for wild animal patients, meet program goals, and further the organization’s mission of protecting and celebrating Oregon’s native wildlife. The position ensures that excellent customer service to volunteers, interns, coworkers, the public, and the patients is consistently administered. An approximate breakdown of those duties can be found below, but is subject to change dependent on the season and needs of the center. 

Animal Care:
Provide care to each patient according to an approved treatment plan as directed by the veterinarian and rehab director. 
Care may include: conducting or supervising exams, providing basic wound  treatment, bandaging (including simple wing wraps), administering fluids and supportive care, accurately dosing and administering medication, performing physical therapy, and other tasks assigned by the veterinarian and/or rehab director.
Hand feeding or tubing of infant/juvenile wildlife patients of all species.
Perform basic lab work such as reading fecals.
Perform euthanasia when necessary, as directed and according to program policy. 
Ensure that patient charts and records are accurately updated.
Potential for advanced care of hospital patients (under the supervision of the rehab director/veterinarian):
Advanced Lab work: Prepare and read blood smear, blood lead test, cytology, and other diagnostics. 
Assist with and/or perform: anesthesia; radiographs; wound cleaning; splints; blood draws; other medical procedures directed by the rehab director/veterinarian. 
Assist veterinarian(s) with scheduled and emergency surgeries. 
Assist with providing medical care for CWC’s ambassador animals according to program policy and/or at the direction of the veterinarian and/or education program directors. 


Daily Support:Supervise teams of interns and volunteers to maximize efficiency and quality of patient care and ensure all work is completed.
Ensure daily cleaning and disinfecting of all areas as necessary to maintain a safe and sanitary environment throughout the hospital and facility. 
Ensure that animal husbandry needs are met for all animals in care including food, dietary supplements, water, enrichment, and enclosure setup. 
Immediately report and document incidents and injuries that occur on shift to the rehab director. 
Staff the wildlife hotline: 
Answer and/or return phone calls as directed, typically to advise a caller on a wildlife conflict (illness, injury, or similar situation).
Recommend solutions which may include hospital admission, referrals to other agencies, supportive care, or no solution needed. 
Log all hotline calls in an online database.
Maintain timely correspondence with team members throughout the day via email, phone, electronic messages, and on-site radios.
Admit new patients: 
 Identify species upon admission.
 Participate in the intake process including intake exam and setting up a patient care plan in collaboration with the veterinarian.
Correspond with the public via e-mail for patient updates.

Operational Support of Wildlife Rehabilitation Clinic:
Attend and participate in staff/program meetings as requested. 
Maintain professional and timely email correspondence from an employer-provided email account. 
Communicate with the director when supplies or other items need to be restocked. 
Identify, report, and/or resolve maintenance issues in a timely manner. Work cooperatively across all departments to accommodate the completion of construction and maintenance projects. 
Work cooperatively as an effective team member with staff and volunteers to ensure the highest standards of animal husbandry, safety, sanitation, and customer service within the hospital, between CWC programs, and out in the community. 
Perform other duties, as assigned, to ensure a positive public image, enhance the operation of the organization, and improve the quality of life for animals in the organization’s care. 



Minimum Qualifications 
At least 18 years of age.
Graduated from high school or received a GED.
Rabies pre-exposure vaccinations or willingness to receive them.
Two or more years of experience in a wildlife rehabilitation setting.
Basic knowledge of wildlife rehabilitation standards including identification, species-specific diet & habitat needs, diagnostics, and restraint.
Commitment to following wildlife rehabilitation standards for quality of life, including the responsible use of euthanasia.
Alignment with CWC’s philosophy on wildlife rehabilitation including policy on non-native species.
Excellent time management skills.
Ability to maintain written records and patient charts.
Strong verbal and written communication & customer service skills.
Ability to foster teamwork, lead by example, approach problems in a solutions-oriented manner, and create a positive work environment through appropriate and timely communication. 
Be punctual, detail-oriented, professional, and dependable.
Willingness to wear a mask both indoors and outdoors as needed.
Willingness to abide by all PPE (personal protective equipment) policies required by clinic policy, including wearing gloves, masks, and using foot baths as needed.
Successful applicants will be required to pass a background check including motor vehicle records.

Preferred Qualifications
Bachelor’s degree in animal science, animal husbandry, biology, zoology, fisheries & wildlife science, or a related area.
Three or more years of experience in wildlife rehabilitation, preferably with species native to Oregon.
Training and/or certification from the IWRC, NWRA, OWRA, or a similar organization.
Knowledge of Oregon’s native flora and fauna.

Working Conditions 

Duties will be performed on Chintimini’s 9.4-acre property which includes grassland, wetland (including a large pond), riparian and deciduous bottomland forest habitats. Must be able to stand for long periods of time, and frequently lift 25-50 pounds. Wildlife Rehabilitation Specialists will be working with live animals, so should be prepared for a job that is as messy as it is rewarding! 

Compensation and Schedule 

Compensation range: $17 - $19 hourly (commensurate to experience), non-exempt.

Schedule: This position is scheduled to work 40 hours, 5 days per week. Includes weekends, some holidays, and evenings.

What CWC Offers: Health insurance, paid sick leave, paid vacation (including rollover vacation and 2 non-rollover personal days per year), 8 designated holidays (or floating holidays if needed), professional development opportunities.

Anticipated start date: September 2026

Contact
Madison Bennett
madison@chintiminiwildlife.org (preferred contact method)
